Pygmalion was a figure from Greek mythology, though he is most famously known from Ovid's "Metamorphoses," a Latin narrative poem. In the story, Pygmalion was a Cypriot sculptor who carved a statue of a woman out of ivory. He was so captivated by his own creation that he fell in love with it. The statue was so lifelike and beautiful that Pygmalion began to treat it as a real woman, dressing it and placing adornments upon it.

In the myth, Pygmalion prayed to the goddess Venus (Aphrodite in Greek mythology) to bring his statue to life. Venus granted his wish, and the statue came to life as a woman named Galatea. Pygmalion and Galatea then married, and the story became a symbol of the power of art and the artist's ability to create something so beautiful and perfect that it could be considered divine.

This myth has been the inspiration for various works of art, literature, and even operas and plays, most notably George Bernard Shaw's play "Pygmalion," which was later adapted into the musical "My Fair Lady."
